warmup.q: The cashback program keeps a table with one row per customer: their current tier. Each purchase looks up its customer's row when it arrives. Mira's 09:30 coffee arrives at 10:01. Her upgrade from silver to gold, made at 10:00, arrived at 10:00. Which tier does the coffee get?
options: Silver: the program matches by the time of the purchase
Gold: the table holds one row per customer, the latest to arrive
None: the purchase is thrown away as late
It depends on how long the table waits for late rows
warmup.why: A plain table keeps only the latest row per customer, by arrival, so the 09:30 coffee is matched with gold. Waiting for late rows exists for this kind of match only when the table keeps its history, and then it's the purchase that waits, not the table. A table that kept its history would answer silver, the tier in force at 09:30. The second section shows why the plain table's answer also changes from one run to the next.

sections.h: Every stream join remembers one side and looks it up with the other
sections.html:
Let's start with a match that every card payment needs. When you tap your card, the shop first asks your bank to set the money aside. That's an authorization. Later, the shop asks for the money to actually move. That's a capture. A petrol pump shows the gap. It asks for up to 100.00 before you fill up, and charges what you really took when you hang up. The payments app writes each authorization to the Kafka topic authorizations and each capture to captures, both keyed by payment id. A topic is a named log in Kafka that programs add records to and read in order, and a record's key is the value it's filed under.

The company wants one line per payment: captured, or never captured. In a database, which keeps finished tables, that's a join: a query that matches rows from two tables on a shared value, here the payment id. You'd write authorizations LEFT JOIN captures USING (payment_id) and run it once. A left join keeps every row of the first table, even the ones with no partner, and those are the never-captured payments.

A stream never finishes. When an authorization arrives at 10:00, its capture may come at 10:04, in three days, or never. It may even come first, if captures happens to be read ahead of the other topic.

The simplest join that could work remembers every record it has ever seen from both sides, filed by key. Each new record looks up the other side's file, emits (sends on) a result for every match, and adds itself to its own file. It gives the right answer, but its memory grows without end: at 3,000 authorizations a second, a year of both topics is about 190 billion records.

So you decide how long a record may still find its partner. That's a window, from Time in streams: a stretch of time with a start and an end. A stream-stream join pairs only records whose timestamps are close enough, and forgets the ones that have fallen out of the window. It measures that in stream time, the largest timestamp the program has seen, not by the wall clock. In Kafka Streams, the library from the last lesson, the window is a JoinWindows:

authorizations.leftJoin(
    captures,
    ValueJoiner { auth, capture -> if (capture == null) "$auth NOT CAPTURED" else "$auth captured $capture" },
    JoinWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(1)),  // either side first, 10 min apart
    StreamJoined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
)

The ValueJoiner builds each output line from the two matched values, and gets null for the capture when there's none. Each side's records wait in a window store on local disk for 10 minutes, plus 1 minute of grace, extra waiting for records that come late. Then they're dropped. A real capture can come days later, and the stored records grow with the window. The left join also answers the question an inner join, which outputs only matches, can't: which authorizations were never captured. It can only say so after the window has closed, so "not captured" comes out late on purpose. Copying the authorization's details into the capture is no substitute. It tells you about captured payments only, and the ones you most want to see have no capture to carry them.

Every stream join keeps state built from one input, and looks it up with the other. State is what a program remembers between records. The kinds of join differ only in how long that state lives, as the figure shows. A stream-stream join keeps a window of each side. A stream-table join keeps the whole table, the latest row per key, and nothing of the stream. A table-table join keeps both tables. Next comes the stream-table join, the one you'll write most often, and the trap in Mira's coffee.

A left join, so an authorization with * no capture comes out too, once its window has closed. */ fun main() { val builder = StreamsBuilder() val captures = builder.stream("captures", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) builder.stream("authorizations", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) .leftJoin( captures, ValueJoiner<String, String?, String> { auth, capture -> if (capture == null) "$auth NOT CAPTURED" else "$auth captured $capture" }, JoinWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(1)), StreamJoined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()), ) .to("auth-outcomes", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) drive(builder.build(), "window-join-demo") { driver -> val auths = driver.createInputTopic("authorizations", StringSerializer(), StringSerializer()) val caps = driver.createInputTopic("captures", StringSerializer(), StringSerializer()) val out = driver.createOutputTopic("auth-outcomes", StringDeserializer(), StringDeserializer()) println("join state: " + driver.allStateStores.keys.sorted()) val arrivals = listOf( Triple("auth", "p-1", "10:00"), Triple("auth", "p-2", "10:01"), Triple("capture", "p-1", "10:04"), Triple("capture", "p-3", "10:05"), Triple("auth", "p-3", "10:03"), Triple("auth", "p-4", "10:20"), Triple("capture", "p-4", "10:22"), ) for ((i, a) in arrivals.withIndex()) { val (kind, payment, time) = a if (kind == "auth") auths.pipeInput(payment, "auth@$time", at(time)) else caps.pipeInput(payment, "@$time", at(time)) val emitted = out.readKeyValuesToList().joinToString { "${it.key}: ${it.value}" } println("%d. %-7s %s at %s -> %s".format(i + 1, kind, payment, time, emitted.ifEmpty { "(nothing yet)" })) } } }

The join keeps three window stores: one per side, plus one for left records still waiting for a match. sections.h: A stream-table join answers with the table as it is now, unless you keep its history
sections.html:
Adding information to each event from a table is called enrichment, and it's the join you'll write most often. Each purchase needs the customer's loyalty tier, because the tier sets the cashback rate: 2% for silver and 5% for gold (made-up rates). The code calls each purchase an order. The tiers live in a database that another part of the company runs. Change data capture turns every change in that database into a record on the topic customer-tiers, keyed by customer id (Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture).

Version 1 asks that database for every order. At 3,000 orders a second and 5 ms per question, that's 15 questions waiting at every moment, and the database has to answer every one. Version 2 keeps a local copy: a KTable built from customer-tiers, which holds the latest value per key in a store on local disk (the last lesson). Each order looks up its customer's row in microseconds. Only orders produce output. A tier update changes the row and emits nothing, so orders already joined keep the tier they got.

Now add time. Customer c-1, Mira from the opening, was silver until 10:00 and gold after. Her order from 09:30 sits in a partition that has fallen behind. (A partition is one of the separate logs a topic is split into, and one can lag behind the others.) It reaches the join at 10:01, after the upgrade. The KTable has one row per customer, so it answers gold, and the order earns cashback that Mira didn't have when she bought.

Worse, the answer depends on arrival order. Rebuild the output next week from the same topics, and the partitions may be read in a different order, so the same order comes out silver. A join whose result depends on arrival order isn't deterministic: two runs over the same data disagree. The stepper walks through it.

The fix is to keep the table's history, and to join each order with the version that was in force at the order's own timestamp. Data warehouses, the databases companies keep for analysis, call this a slowly changing dimension. Kafka Streams (since version 3.5) calls it a versioned table. You keep the table in a versioned store, and a stream-table join then picks the version with the latest timestamp at or before the stream record's timestamp:

val tiers = builder.table("customer-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
    Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("tiers", Duration.ofDays(7))))  // 7 days of history

It has two limits. First, history is bounded. An order more than 7 days older than the table's newest record can't be answered: an inner join drops it, and a left join joins it with nothing (null). Second, versions fix late orders, not late table updates. If the upgrade record itself arrives after an order stamped 10:02, the order gets silver, the latest version known at that moment. A grace period on the stream side, Joined.withGracePeriod(...) on a versioned table, holds each order that long in stream time, so that a slightly late update can still be used. Every order then comes out later by the grace period.

Flink, a program that runs stream jobs across many computers, lets you write them in SQL, and Flink SQL offers the same choices by name. An event-time temporal join, FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time, joins each order with the version of a versioned table valid at that time. It waits for watermarks on both sides (Time in streams), so the watermark plays the grace period's role. A processing-time temporal join uses the latest version, and has the plain table's problem. A lookup join asks an outside database for every row, which is version 1 again.

SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, t.tier
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customer_tiers FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time AS t
  ON o.customer_id = t.customer_id;

Join each event with the table as it was when the event happened, not as it is when the event arrives.

So far, every join had a stream on at least one side. Next, a join with no stream at all.

aside.title: Why not write the tier into each order when it's made?
aside.html: You can, and it's often the best fix. If the program that takes the order looks up the tier and writes it into the order, every later join gets the same answer, because the answer is in the data. Data warehouses do a version of this: they give each version of the tier an id and put that id in the order. The cost is that the order's maker must know the tier at that moment, and every change to how tiers work means changing that program. When the tiers belong to another part of the company, a versioned table is usually easier.

sections.h: A join of two tables is a view that keeps itself up to date
sections.html:
Some joins have no stream side at all. When a card is used, the payment check wants one lookup: from the card to the tier of the account that owns it. Cards come from one part of the company (card id to account id) and tiers from another (account id to tier). Both arrive as changelog topics, where each record is the new value for its key. The output is a table too.

Materialized views and data cubes set up exactly this problem. A materialized view is a stored query result that has to follow its inputs. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW works out the whole join again on a schedule, and is out of date in between. Incremental maintenance applies each change as a small correction instead. A table-table join in a stream program is incremental maintenance that never stops. Each side keeps its table in a state store, and a change on either side is joined with the current state of the other. Written as a formula, with ⋈ for "joined with", it looks like the product rule from calculus:

change(cards ⋈ tiers) = change(cards) ⋈ tiers  +  cards ⋈ change(tiers)

In words: the change in the view is each change to the cards, joined with today's tiers, plus today's cards, joined with each change to the tiers. The program applies one change at a time, so the case where both sides change at once never comes up.

The second half is where the cost hides. One tier change for an account with 4 cards emits 4 view updates. A fee change on a shop category that 200,000 shops belong to would emit 200,000. Deletes come out as tombstones, records with a key and no value. Delete a card, and the view emits card-2 with a null value. A compacted topic downstream, one that keeps only the latest record per key, turns that into a delete (Partitions and segments on disk: retention and compaction).

Kafka Streams has two forms. A KTable-KTable join on the key needs both tables keyed by the same id, and co-partitioned (the next section). A foreign-key join (since Kafka 2.4) joins on a field inside the left table's value. Here the extractor, a small function you pass in, returns the card's account id, which is the key of the tiers table:

cards.join(tiers, Function { account -> account }, ValueJoiner { account, tier -> "$account $tier" })

Kafka Streams sends the changes through internal topics, so that each card meets its account's tier whatever partition either one is in. That costs extra topics, and a round trip through Kafka for every change. Streaming databases such as Materialize and RisingWave build whole SQL views out of joins like these (Unbundling the database: dataflow apps and streaming databases comes back to them).

The plain KTable-KTable join, like the stream-table join, relies on something Kafka can only half check, and that's next.

sections.h: Both sides of a join must land in the same partition, and Kafka checks only half of that
sections.html:
A Kafka Streams program doesn't run one join. It runs one per task, its unit of work for one input partition (the last lesson). Task 0 joins partition 0 of orders with partition 0 of customer-tiers, and sees nothing else. So an order meets its customer's tier only if both records sit in the same partition number. Two things decide that: the number of partitions, and the partitioner, the function that turns a key into a partition number.

The Java producer's partitioner hashes the key's bytes with a function called murmur2, and takes the remainder after dividing by the partition count (Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering). A hash function turns any key into a big number that looks random but is always the same for the same key. Two topics that agree on both the count and the partitioner are co-partitioned.

Change the count, and joins fail without a word. With orders on 3 partitions and tiers on 2, about two keys in three land on a different partition number, so two orders in three find no tier. Kafka Streams catches this one. When the program starts and its tasks are handed out, it compares the partition counts of the topics a join reads, and stops with an error instead of running.

It can't catch a different partitioner. Suppose the tiers come from a program written in Go or Python that uses librdkafka, a widely used Kafka library for languages other than Java. Its default partitioner (consistent_random) hashes keys with a different function, CRC32. With 3 partitions on both sides, two keys in three still land elsewhere, every check passes, and the joins come out with no tier. Set partitioner=murmur2_random in those programs, which the librdkafka documentation describes as matching the Java producer's default.

Growing a topic breaks co-partitioning too. Going from 6 to 12 partitions moves about half of its keys, so every topic you joined it with is now mismatched. It also breaks the order of each key's records, for good measure.

There are three ways out.

  1. Repartition one side to match: repartition(Repartitioned.numberOfPartitions(3)) writes it through an internal topic with the right count, for one extra write and read per record.
  2. For table-table joins, use a foreign-key join, which repartitions on its own.
  3. Make the small side a GlobalKTable, a table that every copy of the program holds in full. Every instance reads all partitions of customer-tiers into a local copy before it handles anything. Then any task can look up any customer, and the join can use any field of the order as the lookup key.

The global table has its price. Every instance stores and reads the whole table: fine for 2 million customers at about 50 bytes each, 100 MB, and not for 2 billion. Start-up waits for the full copy to load. And a GlobalKTable has no idea of time: its joins always use the row it holds now, so the versioned fix from the second section isn't available. The lab has you build both and write the start-up check yourself.

Kafka checks the partition count, not the partitioner. Check the partitioner yourself.

So far, every join matched one record with another. Next, a question about a whole sequence of events.

sections.h: Complex event processing stores the query and lets the data flow past
sections.html:
A database stores data, and runs questions, called queries, that come and go. Complex event processing (CEP) turns that around: the query is stored and lives for a long time, and the events flow past it. Card testing is the classic case. A fraudster, someone using stolen card numbers, tries small purchases until the bank says yes, to learn which cards still work. So "three declines (the bank said no) in a row, then an approval (the bank said yes), within 2 minutes, on one card" is worth an alarm.

You could build that from three windowed joins of the authorization stream with itself. It's simpler as a pattern, turned into a small state machine for each card. A state machine is a program that is always in one of a few states, and moves between them on each event. Here the states are 0, 1, 2 or 3 declines seen. A decline moves one state up. An approval in state 3 is a match, and an approval in any other state goes back to 0. A partial match older than 2 minutes is dropped. The state per card is tiny, the times of up to three declines, and nothing else about the events is kept. The Try it runs that machine in plain Kotlin.

FlinkCEP, Flink's pattern library, says the same thing as a description rather than a machine:

Pattern<Auth, ?> cardTesting = Pattern.<Auth>begin("declines")
        .where(SimpleCondition.of(a -> !a.approved()))
        .times(3).consecutive()                         // three declines in a row
        .next("approval")                               // and the very next event is an approval
        .where(SimpleCondition.of(Auth::approved))
        .within(Duration.ofMinutes(2));                 // all within 2 minutes
PatternStream<Auth> matches = CEP.pattern(auths.keyBy(Auth::card), cardTesting);

next means the very next event of that card, which is called strict contiguity. followedBy would allow other events in between. In event time, FlinkCEP holds events back and checks them in timestamp order as the watermark passes (Time in streams). It treats an event behind the watermark as late: dropped, or sent to a side output. Esper, a CEP engine for Java and Microsoft's .NET that has been around for years, writes patterns in an SQL-like language called EPL. Flink SQL has MATCH_RECOGNIZE, the SQL standard's syntax for patterns across rows.

Search on streams makes the same turn for text. A news-monitoring service stores thousands of saved searches, and matches every new article against all of them. Elasticsearch, a popular search engine, does this with its percolator. You store the queries themselves, in a field of type percolator. Then you send a document, and get back the stored queries it matches. For payments, the stored queries could hold the names of people and companies that the law forbids paying, checked against the name on every new payee:

{ "query": { "percolate": { "field": "rule", "document": { "payee_name": "Northwind Trading LLC" } } } }

The percolator matches every request fresh (it caches nothing), so send documents in batches. Avoid wildcard queries among the stored ones, because they defeat the trick it uses to skip queries that can't match.

That's the limit of every tool in this lesson. Each one keeps state, and you choose how much and for how long, trading memory and delay against missed matches. And a crash in the middle can lose that state or count it twice, which is where the next lesson starts.

try.title: Run a pattern as a state machine
steps: Run CepDemo. It feeds 12 authorization results for four cards through the card-testing pattern, and prints each card's state after every event.
card-4 also has three declines and then an approval. Predict whether it matches, and why.

code.title: CepDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l06.demo import java.time.Duration import java.time.Instant /** One card authorization result. */ data class Auth(val card: String, val approved: Boolean, val at: Instant) /** * A stored query, compiled to a small state machine per card: three declines in a row, then an approval, all within * 2 minutes of the first decline ("card testing": a fraudster tries numbers until one works). The events flow past * it; nothing is stored but each card's partial match. */ class CardTestingPattern(private val within: Duration = Duration.ofMinutes(2)) { /** Per card: the declines seen so far in the current partial match (the state machine's state). */ private val partial = mutableMapOf<String, MutableList<Instant>>() /** Feeds one event; returns a description of the match if this event completes one. */ fun onEvent(e: Auth): String? { val declines = partial.getOrPut(e.card) { mutableListOf() } if (declines.isNotEmpty() && Duration.between(declines.first(), e.at) > within) declines.clear() // too old: drop it if (!e.approved) { declines += e.at if (declines.size > 3) declines.removeAt(0) // keep the three most recent declines return null } val match = if (declines.size == 3) "MATCH ${e.card}: 3 declines from ${hms(declines.first())}, approved at ${hms(e.at)}" else null declines.clear() // an approval ends any partial match return match } fun state(card: String): String = "${partial[card]?.size ?: 0} declines" } fun main() { val t0 = Instant.parse("2026-11-07T10:00:00Z") fun ev(card: String, ok: Boolean, sec: Long) = Auth(card, ok, t0.plusSeconds(sec)) val events = listOf( ev("card-1", false, 0), ev("card-2", true, 5), ev("card-1", false, 20), ev("card-1", false, 41), ev("card-1", true, 50), // card-1: decline, decline, decline, approve in 50 s ev("card-3", false, 60), ev("card-3", false, 70), ev("card-3", true, 80), // only two declines ev("card-4", false, 100), ev("card-4", false, 130), ev("card-4", false, 160), ev("card-4", true, 250), // too slow ) val pattern = CardTestingPattern() for (e in events) { val match = pattern.onEvent(e) println("%s %-7s %-8s state %-10s %s".format(hms(e.at), e.card, if (e.approved) "approved" else "declined", pattern.state(e.card), match ?: "")) } }

try.expect:
10:00:00 card-1  declined state 1 declines
10:00:05 card-2  approved state 0 declines
10:00:20 card-1  declined state 2 declines
10:00:41 card-1  declined state 3 declines
10:00:50 card-1  approved state 0 declines MATCH card-1: 3 declines from 10:00:00, approved at 10:00:50
10:01:00 card-3  declined state 1 declines
10:01:10 card-3  declined state 2 declines
10:01:20 card-3  approved state 0 declines
10:01:40 card-4  declined state 1 declines
10:02:10 card-4  declined state 2 declines
10:02:40 card-4  declined state 3 declines
10:04:10 card-4  approved state 0 declines

card-1 matches: three declines and an approval in 50 seconds. card-3's approval comes after only two declines, so it goes back to 0. card-4 reaches state 3, but its approval comes 150 seconds after the first decline, more than the 2 minutes allowed, so the partial match was dropped. Each card's state never holds more than three timestamps.

refs.title: FlinkCEP 2.3: complex event processing for Flink

opening:
Picture a café chain with a loyalty scheme: silver members get 2% of each purchase back, and gold members get 5%. Mira is upgraded to gold at 10:00. She bought a coffee at 09:30, but that payment was held up, and reached the program that works out cashback at 10:01. The program looks up Mira's tier, finds gold, and gives her 5%.

Next week, the company runs the same program again over the same payments, to check its sums. This time Mira's coffee gets 2%. Same data, same code, two answers.

Looking up the current tier feels like the obvious way to add it to a payment. It's what a join does in a database, where both tables sit still.

In Kafka Streams: tables, state and windows, we added up a stream into a table on local disk. In this lesson, we'll match streams against each other and against tables, see what each kind of match has to remember, and fix Mira's coffee. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with Mira's 09:30 coffee, which got gold cashback one week and silver the next. A plain table answers with whatever row arrived last, so the answer depends on arrival order. A versioned table answers with the tier in force when she paid, every time.

Look at a receipt from a shop where you have a loyalty card. Does it print the points you earned on that purchase? If it does, the shop wrote the answer into the record at the moment you paid, and no later join can change it.

Next, we'll crash a stream program in the middle of its work, and find out what "exactly-once" can really promise.

compare.title: The same as-of join in Kafka Streams and Flink SQL

a.label: Kafka Streams
a.title: versioned table plus grace
a.html: val tiers = builder.table("customer-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()), Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("tiers", Duration.ofDays(7)))) builder.stream("orders", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) .leftJoin(tiers, ValueJoiner { order: String, tier: String? -> "$order tier=${tier ?: "none"}" }, Joined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()) .withGracePeriod(Duration.ofMinutes(5))) // wait for late table updates .to("orders-enriched")

b.label: Flink SQL
b.title: event-time temporal join
b.html: -- customer_tiers is a versioned table: a primary key and an event-time attribute SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, t.tier FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN customer_tiers FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time AS t ON o.customer_id = t.customer_id; -- results wait for the watermarks of both inputs

compare.note: Both pick the version valid at the order's timestamp, and both have to wait for late table updates. They wait on different clocks. Kafka Streams holds each order for a grace period measured in its own stream time, and keeps a limited history (7 days here). Flink waits until the watermarks of both inputs pass the order's time, so the watermark you chose in Time in streams decides how late a tier update may be. Flink also needs the table's primary key, the column that identifies each row, in the join condition. Kafka Streams needs both topics co-partitioned; Flink moves the inputs between its computers by the join key itself.

worked.title: Convert each payment at the exchange rate in force when it was made

steps.say: Name the inputs and their keys. payments is keyed by payment id, and each payment has a currency and an amount. fx-rates holds exchange rates, how many euros one unit of each currency buys, keyed by currency, and each record is stamped with the time the rate took effect. The join key is the currency, so the payments must be given a new key first.
steps.code: val payments = builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde)) .selectKey { _, p -> p.currency } // join on currency, not payment id

steps.say: Make the re-keyed stream co-partitioned with the rates. fx-rates has 6 partitions, so repartition writes the payments through an internal topic with the same count. Then the payment and the rate for USD meet in the same task.
steps.code: val byCurrency = payments.repartition( Repartitioned.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde).withNumberOfPartitions(6).withName("payments-by-currency"))

steps.say: Keep the rates' history. Size it from the longest delay you expect between a payment's timestamp and its arrival: if the program can be a day behind, keep at least a day. Here, 3 days.
steps.code: val rates = builder.table("fx-rates", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Double()), Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("fx-rates", Duration.ofDays(3))))

steps.say: Join with a grace period, because rate updates can arrive late too (here, the rates come in batches every few seconds). Each payment waits 30 seconds of stream time, then uses the rate in force at its timestamp.
steps.code: byCurrency.join(rates, ValueJoiner { p: Payment, rate: Double -> p.copy(amountEur = p.amount * rate) }, Joined.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde, Serdes.Double()).withGracePeriod(Duration.ofSeconds(30))) .to("payments-eur", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))

steps.say: Test the late case, not only the easy one. Send both rates, then a payment stamped between them that arrives after both, then a later payment to move stream time past the grace period. The first payment must use the old rate. Write a second test where the 10:00 rate arrives after a 10:02 payment, and check that the grace period let that payment use it.
steps.code: rateIn.pipeInput("USD", 0.92, at("09:00")) rateIn.pipeInput("USD", 0.95, at("10:00")) paymentIn.pipeInput("p-1", payment(100.0, "USD"), at("09:30")) // a late payment: must use 0.92 paymentIn.pipeInput("p-2", payment(100.0, "USD"), at("10:05")) // moves stream time past 09:30 + 30 s assertThat(out.readValue().amountEur).isCloseTo(92.0, within(0.001))

lab.title: Fix a time-dependent join and check co-partitioning
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests with the command above. Ten of the eleven fail. They need no Kafka: TopologyTestDriver runs your topologies inside the test program.

TierEnrichment.build() is the buggy join from the second section: orders left-joined with a plain, unversioned table of tiers. Read the failing test an order that arrives after the upgrade... and watch it get gold. Fix the table: keep it in a versioned store named STORE, with HISTORY of history. The arrival-order test then runs the same records in 12 random orders and expects one answer.
Write buildGlobal(): the same enrichment against a GlobalKTable, looked up by the order's key.

In CoPartitioning.kt, write partitionFor (the Java producer's formula; a test compares it with the real producer's code), then mismatchShare, then requireCoPartitioned. That last one collects the source topics of every subtopology, each connected piece of the topology, and throws an error if their partition counts differ.

Read the last test, same counts but another partitioner.... It runs your join as three tasks, one per partition, with the tiers placed by CRC32. Your check passes, and most orders still find no tier. Which fix from the fourth section would make it right?
hints: The versioned table: builder.table(TIERS, Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()), Materialized.`as`<String, String>(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore(STORE, HISTORY)).withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.String())).

For the global table, Kotlin needs the store type: Materialized.`as`<String, String, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>(STORE), and the join takes a KeyValueMapper<String, String, String> { customer, _ -> customer } before the joiner.

In requireCoPartitioned: topology.describe().subtopologies(), then sub.nodes().filterIsInstance<TopologyDescription.Source>().flatMap { it.topicSet() }. A global table's source isn't in any subtopology, so the global topology passes on its own.

drill.title: An as-of join from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write a Kafka Streams topology that left-joins orders (keyed by customer) with customer-tiers, so that each order gets the tier in force at its own timestamp, with 7 days of history. Then answer: c-1 has been silver for 30 days and is gold from 10:00 today, and that upgrade is the table's newest record. What do orders stamped 09:59 today, 10:00 today and 8 days ago get?

answer.html: val builder = StreamsBuilder() val tiers = builder.table("customer-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()), Materialized.`as`<String, String>(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("tiers", Duration.ofDays(7))) .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.String())) // keep every version for 7 days builder.stream("orders", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) .leftJoin(tiers, ValueJoiner { order: String, tier: String? -> "$order tier=${tier ?: "none"}" }, Joined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) .to("orders-enriched", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())) // 09:59 today: silver, the latest version at or before 09:59. // 10:00 today: gold. "At or before" includes the version stamped exactly 10:00. // 8 days ago: silver was in force, but that is older than the 7 days of history the store keeps // behind its newest record, so a left join gives tier=none (an inner join would drop the order).

recap: Every stream join keeps state from one input and looks it up with the other. Stream-stream keeps a window of both sides, stream-table keeps the table, and table-table keeps both tables.
A windowed left join can report the record that never found a partner, but only once the window has closed in stream time, so that answer comes late on purpose.

Joining with a table's latest row makes the result depend on arrival order. A versioned table (Kafka Streams 3.5 and later) or a Flink event-time temporal join uses the version in force at the event's time, and a grace period on the stream side covers late table updates.
A table-table join is a view that keeps itself up to date: a change on either side is joined with the other side's current state, so one change to a popular row spreads into many updates.

Partitioned joins need both inputs on the same partition count and the same partitioner. Kafka Streams checks the count at start-up but can't see the partitioner; repartitioning, a foreign-key join or a GlobalKTable avoids the problem.

CEP and search on streams store the query and let the data flow past. The limit of all of these: each keeps state, and you choose how much and for how long, trading memory and delay against missed matches.

explain.prompt: A friend's cashback program joins purchases with a table of customer tiers. After they ran it again over the same data, some purchases got a different cashback rate than the first time. Explain to them what went wrong, how you'd fix it, and what the fix costs.
explain.answer: A plain table keeps one row per customer, whichever arrived last, and each purchase looks it up when the purchase reaches the join. So a purchase made before an upgrade but delivered after it gets the new tier. In the second run, the two topics' partitions were read in a different order, so some purchases saw the other tier: the result depended on arrival order, not on the data. The fix is to join each purchase with the tier in force at the purchase's own timestamp. In Kafka Streams, that means keeping the tiers in a versioned store, which keeps each version with its timestamp for as long as you choose. I'd size that from the longest the program can fall behind. If tier updates can themselves arrive late, I'd add a grace period on the purchase side, so that each purchase waits a little before it's joined. The costs: the store keeps history, so it's bigger, and its changelog can't be compacted down to one row per customer without losing that history. Purchases older than the kept history get no tier. And the grace period delays every purchase's result by that long.

deeper.html:
Interval joins and how long Flink remembers. A Flink SQL regular join (a JOIN b ON a.id = b.id) keeps both inputs in state forever, like the first version in the first section. You can limit it with a time-to-live on the state, at the cost of wrong answers for rows older than that. An interval join adds a time condition on both sides (s.ship_time BETWEEN o.order_time AND o.order_time + INTERVAL '4' HOUR) and needs inputs that are only ever added to. Flink then drops state as the watermark passes, exactly like JoinWindows.

Versions and compaction pull in opposite directions. A compacted changelog keeps only the latest value per key, which is all a plain table needs. A join "as of a time" needs older versions, so the history has to live somewhere: in the versioned store, for as long as it keeps it, or in the events themselves. The data-warehouse trick from the aside, giving each version an id and putting that id in the order, makes later joins give the same answer every time, with no history needed at join time.

Spark. Structured Streaming joins two streams only when you give both sides watermarks and a time condition, so that it can drop state. Lesson 8 of this track covers its watermarks, and its newer real-time mode doesn't support joins of two streams at all.

The book's version. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, covers the three kinds of join and how joins depend on time, with slowly changing dimensions as the data warehouse's answer.
